_about: PRO rewrite pass 5: era-2 scenes 1-39 in play order.

scenarios.title: The Coach for Hire
scenarios.text: A private kicking coach who rebuilt three pro careers offers you his whole offseason: his field, his methods, his famous temper. The price is a number your agent repeats twice.

choices.label: Hire him for the summer
choices.result: The summer belongs to him: brutal drills at dawn, video at night, a temper that softens by July. Your leg feels new by August, and you've never been so tired.

choices.label: Stay with the club's staff
choices.result: The club's staff knows your body, so you stay. It's less glamorous and steady, and the trainers quietly appreciate the vote of confidence.

choices.label: Take most of the summer off
choices.result: Most of the summer, off: lake, family, sleep. You come back rested, a little rusty, and happier than you've been in a long time.

choices.label: Check his record first
choices.result: Two of his former clients, called before you decide. Both rave about the results and warn you about the temper. You hire him with your eyes open, and it shows.

scenarios.title: A College Teammate's Wedding
scenarios.text: Your old college roommate is getting married in June and wants you to give the toast. He's sent a list of stories you're not allowed to tell, and it's longer than the speech.

choices.label: Write a great toast
choices.result: A great toast, written over three weeks and delivered from memory. The bride's grandmother hugs you twice, and the groom mouths 'thank you' from the head table.

choices.label: Tell one true story
choices.result: One true story from freshman year, carefully chosen. It's the one people repeat at breakfast the next morning, and the groom tears up.

choices.label: Remember the pact
choices.result: You raise a glass to the pact you made freshman year. He laughs so hard he can't finish his drink.
choices.lock_text: having made a pact with your college roommate

choices.label: Make peace in the toast
choices.result: You haven't really talked since college. You say so in the toast, and you say sorry. He finds you on the patio afterward.
choices.lock_text: having fallen out with your college roommate

scenarios.title: Wedding Season
scenarios.text: Four friends are getting married this summer, every one of them wants you to give a toast, and three of the weddings are on the same coast in the same month.

choices.label: Give all four toasts
choices.result: Four toasts in five weeks, four suits, four rehearsal dinners. You're exhausted by July and deeply loved, and {best_friend} keeps all four printouts.

choices.label: Write one toast to adapt
choices.result: One great toast structure, adapted four times. It works every time, and only {sibling}, who goes to two of the weddings, notices.

choices.label: Toast once, attend the rest
choices.result: One toast, for the oldest friend, and quiet attendance at the rest. You actually enjoy the other three, dancing badly.

scenarios.title: The Offseason Surgery
scenarios.text: The doctors say a small surgery on your hip now will save your next three seasons. The recovery takes the whole summer: no kicking, a lot of walking, and a lot of waiting.

choices.label: Have the surgery
choices.result: Surgery in May, and a long, boring summer of walking and bands. By camp your hip is better than it's been in years, and you kick without thinking about it.

choices.label: Train through it
choices.result: No surgery: you train through it. It holds, for now, and the doctor writes something in your file that you can't read upside down.

choices.label: Get a second opinion
choices.result: A second opinion, and a month to decide. The second doctor agrees with the first, and the month helps you make peace with it.

scenarios.title: The Training Partner
scenarios.text: A young kicker from a rival club asks to train with you this summer. He's talented, nervous, and says he's watched every one of your kicks since he was in high school.

choices.label: Train together
choices.result: All summer, together. You both get better, you make a friend, and you think twice about it every time your clubs play.

choices.label: Keep your secrets
choices.result: No, politely. You don't help the competition, and you train alone all summer, a little harder and a little lonelier.

choices.label: Make it a summer camp
choices.result: A group of four kickers instead, from four clubs. It becomes an unofficial summer camp that runs for years, and you're its first coach.

scenarios.title: The Class
scenarios.text: You sign up for an evening class at the community college, something that has nothing to do with football: astronomy, it turns out, with a professor who has never heard of you.

choices.label: Earn the A
choices.result: Every reading, every lab, every telescope night. You get an A, and the class is the best part of your week all spring.

choices.label: Bring {backup} along
choices.result: {backup} comes too, grumbling. You study together in the facility cafeteria, and by finals {backup} knows more constellations than you.

choices.label: Audit it for fun
choices.result: Audited, no grades and no pressure. You just look at the stars on Thursday nights, and it's the most peaceful part of your week.

choices.label: Take the next step
choices.result: With your degree finished, you take a graduate-level class instead. It's hard, the reading is endless, and you love every page of it.

scenarios.title: The Summer Without Football
scenarios.text: For one offseason, you put the kicking bag in the closet and decide not to touch a ball for six weeks. On day three, your leg starts to itch.

choices.label: Keep the bag in the closet
choices.result: Six weeks, untouched. You read, travel and sleep, and when you finally open the closet, you come back hungry in a way you'd forgotten.

choices.label: Spend it with family
choices.result: All six weeks with family: the lake house, {parent}'s birthday, {sibling}'s new apartment. It's the best summer you've had in years.

choices.label: Study the greats
choices.result: Film of the best kickers in history instead of kicking. You fill a notebook and come back with three ideas, one of them good.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Coach Calls
scenarios.text: Your old private kicking coach calls out of nowhere with an idea about your plant foot. He's been watching your games, he says, and something has been bothering him since October.

choices.label: Work on his idea
choices.result: A week of working on his idea, charting everything. It helps, a half-step and a little more lift, and you send him the numbers.

choices.label: Visit him for a day
choices.result: A day at his field, just like old times: his whistle, your kicks, his coffee. You both leave happier than you expected.

choices.label: Thank him and keep your form
choices.result: A warm thank-you, and you keep your form as it is. He understands, mostly, and keeps watching your games from his couch.

scenarios.title: The Charity Golf Event
scenarios.text: The club's charity golf event: donors in expensive shoes, owners in carts, and one teammate who's had far too much sun and keeps trying to drive the cart into the pond.

choices.label: Charm the donors
choices.result: Eighteen holes with the donors, your worst golf and your best stories. The charity raises more than last year, and one donor sends you a handwritten note.

choices.label: Look after the teammate
choices.result: The sunburned teammate gets water, shade and a ride home from you. He doesn't remember most of it and thanks you anyway on Monday.

choices.label: Play your round and go
choices.result: Your round, a sandwich, and home by three. Your golf is terrible, nobody asks you for anything, and you nap.

scenarios.title: The Off-Season Weight
scenarios.text: You come back from the offseason six pounds heavier than the club likes. The strength coach is waiting by the scale with a clipboard and a face like a disappointed uncle.

choices.label: Step on the scale
choices.result: On the scale, number read out loud, and six weeks of earning the old one back. It's miserable, and your legs feel lighter by the opener.

choices.label: Bring your own numbers
choices.result: Your summer leg-speed numbers, printed and highlighted. They're better than last year, and the strength coach backs off a little, grudgingly.

choices.label: Joke with the strength coach
choices.result: Jokes, a confession about the ice cream, and an agreement on a plan. The strength coach likes you more for it and doubles your sprints.

scenarios.title: The Homecoming Event
scenarios.text: Your high school invites you back for its homecoming game. They want you at the pep rally, on the field at halftime, and in the trophy case photo with your old coach.

choices.label: Walk the halls with {parent}
choices.result: The halls, with {parent}, in the afternoon. A teacher still has your old essay about wanting to be a kicker, and reads it aloud.

choices.label: Talk to the team
choices.result: The football team before the game, in the old locker room. The kicker can't stop grinning, and you leave him your cleats.

choices.label: Send a halftime video
choices.result: A video, played at halftime on the old scoreboard. They cheer anyway, and someone films the crowd cheering for you and sends it.

scenarios.title: The Offseason Media Tour
scenarios.text: Your growing reputation comes with an offseason full of interview requests: podcasts, morning shows, and a magazine that wants to photograph you on a beach.

choices.label: Say yes to most
choices.result: Most of them, yes. Your name is everywhere by June, your phone never stops, and you're more tired than in season.

choices.label: Do three, and do them well
choices.result: Three interviews, carefully chosen and well prepared. One of them becomes the clip people share whenever your name comes up.

choices.label: Keep the summer quiet
choices.result: A quiet summer and your training, no interviews. Nobody photographs you on a beach, which suits you fine, and your agent sighs.

scenarios.title: The Long Offseason
scenarios.text: The longest offseason of your career: fourteen weeks with no games, no meetings and nowhere to be. By week two you've reorganized the garage twice.

choices.label: Rest for real
choices.result: Real rest, for once: no plans, long walks and long naps. Your body thanks you, and the garage stays organized.

choices.label: Take a course
choices.result: A course in something you've always wondered about: woodworking, it turns out. You make a crooked table and love it.

choices.label: Travel with family
choices.result: Three weeks of travel with the people you love most. It's the longest you've been away from a ball since high school.

scenarios.title: The Hometown Kids' Camp
scenarios.text: You run a free camp for kids in your hometown: two days, two hundred kids, one field, a donated pallet of footballs and the old high school band.

choices.label: Run every station
choices.result: Every station, run by you. You lose your voice by noon on day one and keep going in a whisper, and the kids love the whisper.

choices.label: Bring three teammates
choices.result: Three teammates, including {holder}. The kids lose their minds, and {holder} runs a holding clinic that's the hit of the weekend.

choices.label: Make it a yearly camp
choices.result: The high school becomes a partner, so the camp happens every year whether you're there or not. It's the most lasting thing you've built.

scenarios.title: The Fitness Test
scenarios.text: The club's offseason fitness test: shuttle runs, a mile, a jump. You're not where you were, the strength coach writes your times down without comment, and the linemen are watching.

choices.label: Train for the retest
choices.result: Three weeks of training for the retest, and you pass it clean, faster than last year. The linemen cheer, sarcastically and then sincerely.

choices.label: Explain kicking fitness
choices.result: Your leg numbers, shown to the trainers: kicking fitness isn't running fitness. They agree, mostly, and adjust your test for next year.

choices.label: Accept the number
choices.result: The number is the number. You accept it calmly and plan a better summer, and the strength coach nods, clearly surprised.

scenarios.title: The Kicker Brought In
scenarios.text: The club signs a kicker with a bigger leg and a lower salary and puts him at the locker next to yours. He's polite, twenty-three, and kicks sixty-yarders in warmups for fun.

choices.label: Out-prepare him
choices.result: Every day, better prepared than him. He has the leg; you have the habits. By October the coaches have noticed which one matters.

choices.label: Get to know him
choices.result: Lunch, then dinner, then a friendship. He's nervous and decent, and you both kick better without the tension in the room.

choices.label: Ask {coach} the plan
choices.result: The plan, asked for straight out in the hallway. {coach}'s answer is honest: it's an open competition. It stings, and it helps to know.

scenarios.title: Don't Talk About It
scenarios.text: The specialists have a superstition: nobody says the streak out loud. A rookie just said it at lunch, loudly, with the whole table listening, and the snapper has put down his fork.

choices.label: Laugh and reassure him
choices.result: Laughing, you tell the rookie it's fine. The room relaxes, the snapper picks up his fork, and the streak goes on.

choices.label: Change absolutely nothing
choices.result: Your routine stays exactly the same, down to the socks, the parking spot and the brand of gum. The specialists approve in total silence.

choices.label: Make the rookie buy lunch
choices.result: Lunch for the specialists, every day for a week, on the rookie. It becomes a tradition, and he takes it well.

scenarios.title: The Incentive Clause
scenarios.text: Your contract pays a bonus if you hit ninety percent this season, and your agent keeps texting you the math: where you are, what's left, what one miss would mean.

choices.label: Ask your agent to stop
choices.result: No more math, please, you text back. You'll find out at the end of the season, and the next three months are quieter.

choices.label: Chase the number
choices.result: The number goes on your locker, and you chase it every practice. It's motivating, and some nights it's all you can think about.

choices.label: Forget the bonus
choices.result: Forgotten, on purpose, and the agent's texts go unread. If it comes, it comes, and you kick more freely than you have in years.

scenarios.title: The Bad Week
scenarios.text: You snapped at {holder} in practice, walked past {coach} without a word and skipped the team meal. It's Wednesday, and it's been that kind of week.

choices.label: Apologize to {holder}
choices.result: A real apology to {holder} before practice, no excuses. The holds are better that afternoon, and {holder} buys you a coffee.

choices.label: Tell {coach} what's going on
choices.result: What's actually going on comes out in {coach}'s office: sleep, family, the pressure. The coach listens and gives you a lighter week.

choices.label: Take one night completely off
choices.result: One night, completely off: no film, no phone, no football, just a long walk and a bad movie. It resets you, and Thursday is a better day.

scenarios.title: The Agent's Bigger Client
scenarios.text: Your agent just signed a star quarterback. Your last three calls went to voicemail, and the fourth went to an assistant who asked how to spell your last name.

choices.label: Say something now
choices.result: A short email to your agent: what you need this year, and by when. The reply comes from the agent personally, a day late and genuinely apologetic, with a meeting date.

choices.label: Let it slide
choices.result: The agent's busy, you tell yourself, and it'll even out. It doesn't. You stop expecting calls back, and you start finding out things from reporters.

choices.label: Vent to the locker room
choices.result: Complaints about your agent, to anyone who'll listen. Two teammates say theirs is worse, and a reporter hears about all of it by Friday.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Traded Away
scenarios.text: The club traded your holder's best friend at midnight. {holder} found out from a phone notification, sitting in the parking lot after practice, and hasn't said much since.

choices.label: Check on {holder}
choices.result: First thing in the morning, you find {holder}, and you stay through lunch. Nothing much is said, and it helps.

choices.label: Talk to the specialists
choices.result: A few words to the specialists about how the business works, and how to look after each other in it. The young ones need it.

choices.label: Keep your head low
choices.result: It's the business, and you know it could be you. You keep your head low and your phone face down.

scenarios.title: The Big Check
scenarios.text: Your signing bonus clears on a Tuesday. Within an hour your phone lights up with cousins, a car dealer, two realtors and someone from high school who wants to 'catch up'.

choices.label: Put it somewhere boring
choices.result: You put almost all of it somewhere boring and tell everyone it's tied up. Nobody believes you, and nobody can get to it.

choices.label: Celebrate properly
choices.result: The whole family, on a trip, and then the house with the pool. It's the best summer anyone in your family has had, and the pool bill arrives in September.

choices.label: Set aside a family share
choices.result: You set aside one share for family and tell them it's the only one. The cousins grumble. {parent} quietly approves.

scenarios.title: The Restaurant
scenarios.text: An old college teammate wants your name and your money on a steakhouse downtown. He has a chef, a location and a business plan he wrote last night, and he keeps saying 'can't miss.'

choices.label: Put your money in
choices.result: You sign the papers at his kitchen table. Your name goes up in lights in March, and you eat there twice a week because it's yours.

choices.label: Ask to see real numbers
choices.result: A real plan, the lease and an accountant's review, please. He's offended, sends half of it, then stops answering. You keep your money and lose some of a friendship.

choices.label: Lend your name, not your money
choices.result: The opening night, a photo line and nothing more: your name, not your money. He's disappointed and says so, then takes the deal.

choices.label: Send it to your advisor
choices.result: Your advisor reads the plan in an afternoon and circles four things that would sink it. You send the list to your old teammate as a favor. He fixes two of them and opens without you.

scenarios.title: The Friend's Start-Up
scenarios.text: {best_friend} is starting a company, a real one with a plan, a lawyer and two hires, and asks you over dinner to be the very first investor. They've practiced the pitch.

choices.label: Invest
choices.result: You write the check because it's {best_friend}, and because the plan is actually good. You get a seat at their first board meeting and don't understand half of it.

choices.label: Invest a little, and say why
choices.result: You invest a small piece and tell {best_friend} why it's small. It stings for a day, and they respect it after that.

choices.label: Say no as a friend
choices.result: You say you don't mix friendship and money, and you mean it kindly. {best_friend} says they understand, and calls a little less often.

scenarios.title: {parent}'s House
scenarios.text: You could pay off {parent}'s mortgage this week with one transfer. He's told you not to, twice, in the voice he used when you were twelve.

choices.label: Do it anyway
choices.result: You pay it off and tell him after. He's furious for an hour and doesn't speak at dinner. A month later, he still has the letter from the bank on his fridge.

choices.label: Ask what he'd accept
choices.result: You ask {parent} what he would actually accept. He agrees to a loan with no interest, insists on paying it back, and pays it back early.

choices.label: Respect his wish
choices.result: You respect his wish and let it go. He's proud of that, in his quiet way, and you send money to his church instead.

choices.label: Do it the way that worked before
choices.result: You set it up the way you did last time: quietly, through the bank, with his name on everything. He grumbles and signs.
choices.lock_text: having helped your family with money before

scenarios.title: {parent} Is Getting Older
scenarios.text: {parent} forgets the name of a neighbor he's known for twenty years, in the middle of a story on the phone. He laughs it off. You don't.

choices.label: Go home for the bye
choices.result: Home for the bye weekend, every minute with him: the hardware store, the porch, the old stories. He tells the neighbor story right this time.

choices.label: Find him a specialist
choices.result: A specialist, found and booked, and you join the first appointment by video. It's probably nothing, the doctor says, and you hold on to 'probably'.

choices.label: Call every other day
choices.result: Every other day, a phone call, ten minutes or an hour. It's not much, it's something, and he starts saving stories for you.

scenarios.title: {sibling}'s Own Shot
scenarios.text: {sibling} has a tryout of his own, with a semi-pro team three hours from home, and he wants you there. He's never asked you for anything before.

choices.label: Be at the fence
choices.result: A flight in, and you stand behind the fence all morning. He looks for you before every kick, and finds you every time.

choices.label: Coach him by phone
choices.result: The night before, by phone: one thought, one routine, nothing else. He calls after the tryout to tell you it worked, and he sounds like a different person.

choices.label: Send a message and watch later
choices.result: A message in the morning, the video at night. He understands, mostly, and doesn't mention it again, which tells you something.

choices.label: Tell him what you learned
choices.result: You tell {sibling} the hardest thing you ever learned: show up, tell the truth, let the rest go. Then you're there at the fence.
choices.lock_text: having learned what showing up means

scenarios.title: {tyler} Gets Cut
scenarios.text: {tyler} is released on a Monday morning. He calls you before he calls his agent, and for a long time neither of you says anything.

choices.label: Listen for an hour
choices.result: An hour on the phone, mostly listening. He doesn't want advice, and you don't give any, and he thanks you twice.

choices.label: Make a call for him
choices.result: A special teams coach you know gets a call from you, and you say {tyler}'s name twice. He has a workout by Friday.

choices.label: Promise to talk soon
choices.result: A message, warm and short, and a promise to talk soon. You mean it, and it still takes three weeks before you actually call.

scenarios.title: The Holder's Last Season
scenarios.text: {holder} is retiring after this season and wants every hold to count. They've started bringing a notebook to practice, writing down each one, with the date and the weather.

choices.label: Celebrate every practice
choices.result: Every practice becomes a small celebration: a joke, a photo, a cake on the fortieth birthday. {holder} cries twice, happily.

choices.label: Make every kick count
choices.result: Every kick in practice, for {holder}, like it's the playoffs. The notebook fills up with good ones, and {holder} reads them to you on Fridays.

choices.label: Train the next holder
choices.result: The next holder gets trained by both of you, all season, so the job is in good hands. {holder} calls it the best thing you ever did for them.

scenarios.title: The Concussion
scenarios.text: A teammate who has had too many concussions takes another hit in practice and hides it. You saw it happen, and he saw you see it.

choices.label: Tell the trainers
choices.result: The trainers hear it from you before the next drill. He's angry for a week and won't look at you, then thanks you in the parking lot.

choices.label: Talk to him first
choices.result: Away from everyone, by the water cooler, you convince him to tell the trainers himself. It costs you an hour and some of his pride.

choices.label: Look the other way
choices.result: Looking the other way, you let it go. He plays the next game, and you watch him every single snap, wondering if you were wrong.

scenarios.title: The Veteran Who Can't Let Go
scenarios.text: A thirty-six-year-old linebacker is getting cut on Friday, and he hasn't figured it out yet. He's still planning next year's offseason out loud at lunch.

choices.label: Sit with him on his last day
choices.result: Lunch with him on his last day, just the two of you. He talks about his first season the whole time, and you let him.

choices.label: Get the young players to say goodbye
choices.result: The young players, quietly told to say goodbye before he's gone. Twenty of them line up at his locker, and he can't speak.

choices.label: Let it happen
choices.result: It's not your place, so you let it happen. It stays with you, the empty chair at lunch, longer than you expect.

scenarios.title: The Players-Only Meeting
scenarios.text: The team captains call a players-only meeting about {coach}'s boss, the head coach, and they want every player's vote. For the first time, they're asking the kicker.

choices.label: Speak honestly
choices.result: Tough and fair, you say about the head coach, and you give two examples. Some agree, some don't, and the vote is closer because of you.

choices.label: Ask for the facts first
choices.result: What exactly is the problem? The meeting gets calmer as people answer, and the vote becomes a list of fixes instead.

choices.label: Abstain
choices.result: An abstention. Kickers rarely get asked anyway, and you'd rather not start now. The captains notice, and they stop asking you for a while.

scenarios.title: The Player Rep
scenarios.text: The team needs a players' union representative, the job of standing up in front of management twice a year. Nobody wants to be the one management remembers.

choices.label: Volunteer
choices.result: Volunteered. It's meetings and conference calls, and the young players start coming to you with questions about everything from contracts to pensions.

choices.label: Nominate the right person
choices.result: The veteran who should do it gets nominated by you. He accepts, grumbling, and does it brilliantly for three years.

choices.label: Leave it to someone else
choices.result: Someone else does it. You vote for them and go back to kicking, relieved, a little guiltily, every time there's a meeting.

scenarios.title: The Injured Teammate
scenarios.text: A teammate who tore his knee for the team last season is cut the day he's cleared to practice. He found out in the training room, still wearing the brace.

choices.label: Help him clean out his locker
choices.result: His locker, cleaned out with your help, into two cardboard boxes. He doesn't say much, and he hugs you at the car.

choices.label: Say something to the room
choices.result: A few words to the room about how this business works and what we owe each other inside it. The young players listen closely.

choices.label: Keep quiet
choices.result: Quiet. You're one bad season from the same thing, and you know it, and you kick a little angrier that week.

scenarios.title: The Leak
scenarios.text: Someone is leaking locker-room conversations to a beat reporter, word for word, and the coaches think it's a specialist. The punter is furious. So is {holder}.

choices.label: Find the pattern
choices.result: Which details leak, and when? You notice the pattern and tell {coach}: it's a rookie lineman with a cousin at the paper.

choices.label: Rally the specialists
choices.result: The specialists, gathered: everyone knows what's at stake, and nobody says anything outside the room. {holder} calls it a team meeting.

choices.label: Let the coaches sort it
choices.result: The coaches will sort it out, you decide. They do, slowly, and the specialists' room stays tense and quiet for a month.

scenarios.title: The Prime Slump
scenarios.text: You're supposed to be at your best, and the misses in practice have started making headlines. The coaches haven't said anything about it yet, which is worse.

choices.label: Go back to the film
choices.result: You go back to the film of your best season and find the one thing that changed: your plant foot drifted half an inch. It takes a week to fix.

choices.label: Kick two hundred a day
choices.result: You kick through it, two hundred extra balls a day. Your leg aches, your rhythm comes back, and nobody can say you didn't work.

choices.label: Lean on the holder
choices.result: You and {holder} go back to basics together, laughing at how far you've come. It helps more than you expected.

choices.label: Use the tools you learned
choices.result: The tools you learned the last time this happened come right back: the breath, the word, the one thought. The slump is shorter this time, by a lot.

scenarios.title: Untouchable
scenarios.text: Your streak is the longest in the league, the highlight shows run it every Sunday, and the other team's kicker catches you on the field after warmups to ask for tips.

choices.label: Share a tip
choices.result: One real tip, about his follow-through. He thanks you publicly the next week, and the league notices what kind of veteran you are.

choices.label: Don't talk about the streak
choices.result: Not a word about the streak, to anyone, including him. He laughs, says he understands completely, and walks away shaking his head.

choices.label: Enjoy it quietly at home
choices.result: A good dinner at home, the highlights off, the streak unmentioned. You enjoy it the way you'd want to remember it.

scenarios.title: Hurt in Your Prime
scenarios.text: A hip flexor strain, in the best season of your career. The club wants to know how long, the reporters want to know how bad, and the trainers want you to stop asking.

choices.label: Follow the plan exactly
choices.result: The trainers' plan, exactly, every day. You're back right on schedule, and the hip feels stronger than it did before the strain.

choices.label: Push to come back early
choices.result: Early, by a week, and sore. You kick through it, and the trainers keep a very close eye on you all month.

choices.label: Take the full time and more
choices.result: The full recovery time and then a few days more. You come back fresh and fully healed, and a little behind.

choices.label: Build the plan with the trainers
choices.result: This time you build the plan with the trainers, using everything you learned last time. You're back early and healthy, and the trainers start asking your advice.
choices.lock_text: having been through a hard recovery before

scenarios.title: The Rookie Asks
scenarios.text: A rookie specialist catches you after practice with a question you used to ask yourself: how do you stop thinking about the last kick? He looks like he hasn't slept.

choices.label: Answer it fully
choices.result: You answer it fully and stay an hour, showing him the breathing and the one thought. He asks you something new every week after.

choices.label: Take him to dinner
choices.result: Dinner, your treat, and every question answered. He's homesick, too, which you can hear between the questions, and you invite him to Thanksgiving.

choices.label: Give him one line
choices.result: You give him a short answer and go home. On the drive you think of a better one, and you tell him in the morning.
